accuracy.evidence: Checked against the NC England KS3 physics light statements (ray model for mirror images, refraction, convex lens focusing), BBC Bitesize KS3/GCSE reflection and refraction pages and the Institute of Physics 'Light' teaching guidance. Recomputed with Snell's law and n = 1.5 (crown glass is about 1.52): 40° in air gives 25.4° in glass, 25° in glass gives 39.3° in air, block angles 20°→13°, 40°→25°, 60°→35°, each leaving at its entry angle; plane-mirror image distance equals object distance (20 cm and 35 cm; 2 m from the mirror means 4 m from the image); 30° to the surface is a 60° angle of incidence; a fatter convex lens has a shorter focal length. The lens screen is shown in drawing units, not invented centimetres.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented ray-diagram errors (Institute of Physics Supporting Physics Teaching: Light; Guesne in Driver et al., Children's Ideas in Science; AQA examiner reports): measuring angles from the surface, taking the angle of reflection as the angle between the rays, placing the image on the mirror or at twice the distance, mixing up towards and away from the normal, believing a ray along the normal bends, drawing solid rays behind a mirror, and expecting a block to bend the ray further. Each has its own message.

lab_distinct.evidence: gate_lab_distinct passed under the 30% shingle limit, including flag_ray.js (light travels in straight lines, ages 10–11), flag_shine.js (reflecting light, which surfaces reflect), flag_bounce.js and flag_wave.js. No other lab aims a ray at a target with angles from the normal, places a virtual image where traced-back rays meet, chooses refracted paths for three boundary cases with Snell's-law angles, fires rays through a parallel-sided block, or moves a screen to focus thin and fat convex lenses.

lab_teaches.evidence: Six steps: drag the torch (or ±10° buttons) until the reflected ray hits a star at 50°, with i, r and the angle to the mirror shown; drag a ghost candle until the dashed back-traced rays line up (two distances); pick the true path from three candidates for air→glass, glass→air and along-the-normal; fire through a glass block at three angles and see the emerging ray parallel to the dashed continuation of the incident ray; move a screen until three parallel rays make a sharp dot for a thin and then a fat lens; then the challenge.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 30° to the surface read as a 30° angle of incidence, the image 'on the mirror surface' or at 40 cm, the ray from a block 'bent even more', and a fatter lens focusing further away. Each is then tested in the lab and the reveal repeats the learner's choice.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions (reflection from the normal, reflection from the surface, air into glass, along the normal, distance to your image, dashed lines behind a mirror) with rotated answer order. Ten distinct wrong-answer messages: measured from the surface, angle between the rays, the wrong way round, no bend at an angle, a ray along the normal bending, reflecting straight back, distance to the mirror only, halfway, real rays behind a mirror, image on the glass.

readability.evidence: validate_lessons readability passed (kid about 3.4 and adult about 5.1 by learn/readability.py, limits 6.5 and 9.5). Normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, image, refraction and principal focus are defined in short sentences where first used; lab banners are one or two sentences that wrap inside the canvas at 360 px.

no_filler.evidence: No filler patterns matched (gate_content). Kid paragraphs each do one job: draw the normal and measure from it, the law of reflection with a worked 30°/60° case, finding a mirror image, refraction and the convex lens. Adult text gives the standard, the checked figures and the named mistakes.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 × 640 (2x) in light and dark themes for every step. First sheets showed the i/r labels on top of the rays, overlapping A/B circles in the refraction step, and the block's exit ray running off the canvas and through the angle buttons; labels moved to a legend under the banner, candidate circles were set at different radii, and block rays are clipped to the canvas above the buttons. Finished steps now keep their final scene instead of going blank.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (torch ±10°, ghost nearer/further, Path A/B/C, Fire at 0/20/40/60°, screen nearer/further). The canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the angles, ghost distance, case, block angles or screen position. The browser gate ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) on desktop and iPhone 13 in both themes with no violations; the wrong-path click sweep raised no console errors.
